Unpacking the CA report on the Huey accidents

By: Michael Duffett | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
Last year a Working on Fire huey helicopter crashed whilst fighting fires. A week later, another one went down, also killing the pilot. Recently the CA released their findings on the cause for the first accident which is resulting in the deceased pilot's wife contemplating legal action. It found that working on fire maintenance was not up to scratch and that the pilot erred in not doing preflight checks and acting quickly when a light came on in the cockpit warning of gearbox failure. The CA report is being challenged by Working on Fire. We unpack the report using other experts such as a veteran helicopter pilot who has fought fires often himself. He will use his own huey helicopter as an example when chatting about the accidents and the report. For example the report says that the pilot should have noticed frayed cables but these are actually hidden underneath panels. Our case study Mr Jannie Smit will demonstrate this. He will also take us for a spin in his huey helicopter where some of the interviews will be done.

This investigation will be set within a narrative about the huey helicopter and why they are so popular in South Africa. But they are controversial which we will touch upon. Our pilot will tell us that there is little doubt that in massive fires like the Cape has witnessed, it is little wonder that these huey helicopters experience extreme stress and that maintenance has to be a priority. The pilot continues to say that more fire fighting helicopter pilots will die because a lot of them lack the experience in firefighting.

Right after the accident, the working on fire huey helicopters were grounded and all had to be checked, now maintenance is spread over several other companies, but the question remains: Working on Fire has massive contracts from thr govt. How is it possible that they only had 2 registered engineers whose job was to cover and inspect all 20 huey Helicopters? Was this cost saving?

Further information:
Will confirm these interviews by tomorrow afternoon.

Press Release:


Aircraft Maintenance Under Fire
It’s fire season in Cape Town and firefighters have been working around the clock to respond to as many as 4500 fires since November last year. But three fatal aircraft accidents in just 7 months have left a barrage of burning questions about the maintenance schedules on aircraft used to fight fires. Carte Blanche investigates.


Script:


It’s cape town fire season again. Massive fires, fuelled by gale force winds have consumed vast hectares of land and properties over thee last few weeks. Risking their lives are brave firefighters on the ground and in the air. Jannie Smith a pilot, who has experience in aerial fighting knows the dangers.

Jannie: it's when the winds are really bad, you have really a lot of smoke, up and down drafts, and then these pilots have to go and do what they do best, is try to put that fire out. So for them it's very difficult, it's very dangerous,

Recently The Visage family visited the crash site where brother and son Jastun lost his life 20 months ago. He was in a huey helicopter which crashed into the mountain side in the Boland. Debris from the crash still lay there, a grim reminder of the tragedy.

John Hollies: He was a very good son to me. Anything that I asked him to do in life for me he would do for me.

The crash also claimed the life of pilot Darrel Rea. A month earlier another Huey helicopter crashed at cape Point killing pilot Willem Hendrik Marais affectingly known as Bees. And, six months before that high respected veteran pilot Richard Aschenborne was killed in Mpumalanga when his fixed wing water bomber plane crashed.

Inge: I don't know how you cope. I think it is terrible. There is not a day when I don’t think about him.

Three fatal accidents over a 7-month period. All aircraft were operated and maintained by Working on Fire’s associated company the FFA, that’s the the Forest Fire Association. It is now known as Kishugu Aviation.

Mr. Abrahams as a company you must have been devastated by three fatal accidents in such a short period of time.
Abrahams: I think those accidents were a tragic event to us and really shook the company. We have been flying for 30 years with almost 30 000 hours without any fatalities. So we a family. Our pilots, our engineers, our firefighters. So it was a huge loss and huge shakeup

Trevor Abrahams, previously commissioner for the civil aviation authority heads up Working on Fire. Its a job creating initiative which has boots on the ground. And it has a large aerial fleet comprising of spotter planes, water bombers and 14 huey helicopters.

LINK: The huey helicopter is synonymous with the Vietnam war where it gained a reputation as the backbone of the American military effort. All these years later its still in use because of its reliability and the fact that its an incredibly forgiving aircraft.

Jannie owns two of them, similar to the ones operated by working on Fire.

JANNIE: The huey helicopter is a very, very hardy, strongly built machine. One must remember that these machines were built to fight a war. If you look after it well, if you grease it well, you do the services and the maintenance as you want. You do your inspections daily, there's not much that can go wrong.

But it went tragically wrong for legendary pilot Bees Marais who had 11000 flying hours under his belt and was highly popular amongst his peers and colleagues.

Chris: An incredible, incredible person. Always loyal, always fun. I never saw him miserable.

In March 2015 carte blanche aired a story on the terrible fires that ravaged the cape peninsula destroying properties and laying waste to 7000 hectares of vegetation. On the morning of the broadcast Bees Marais was fighting fires at cape point because one had flared up there again. A warning light came on in the cockpit. Before he could perform an emergency landing land, the helicopter crashed into the ground, bursting into flames. Bees was killed instantly. A stunned flying community attended his memorial service. Hs wife Jackie, friends and colleagues remain devastated.

Chris: First of all, without any doubt whatsoever, that I know that Bees wouldn’t make a mistake. Bees was always careful. He was an incredible pilot and I was utterly shocked, absolutely shocked.

Darrel Rea, was the chief pilot of working on fire. Brilliant and gifted at flying, he rose quickly through the ranks. He was married to Angela and together they had baby boy.

ANGELA: Very loving. Quite quiet and not a big socialiser. He preferred to be with his family but very hard working.

According to Angela he was deeply concerned about maintenance issues surrounding the Working on fire aerial fleet. She recalls a tense phone call her husband made.

ANGELA: I can’t say if it was a few weeks or a few days before the accident but he had phoned the chief engineer at WOF and was you know saying his concerns and he was like “Really we have to do something about this.”

A month after Bees Marais died, a huge dire broke out on Bain’s Kloof pass. Daryl was on duty and alongside him was fire safety officer Jastun Visagie. His huey unexpectedly crashed into the hill side. News leaked through to Angela about the accident. That evening friends arrived at her doorstep.

ANGELA: I just started screaming at Marc saying, “Tell me he is okay!” So obviously he said, “Sorry I can’t...”

What upsets Angela most is that 5 months earlier, Darryl had written an email to kishugu aviation after he had chaired a meeting with fellow pilots. HE said “The risk of an accident occurring in one of our aircraft due to maintenance has become unacceptably high” He went on to express concern about the shortage of engineers, a shortage of spares and the lack of the auditing and monitoring of incidents, accidents and snags. We asked Trevor Abrahams about the email.

TREVOR ABRAHAMS: He raised that matter with management in a meeting as I understand it in Newlands and as a result of that various steps were taken to address the issues that he had raised.
JOHN: And then he died?
TREVOR ABRAHAMS: Well he died quite a bit after that in another accident.

One Kishugu ex employee told us that Daryl and Jastun’s deaths were the final straw especially so soon after the deaths of Richard Ashenborn and bees marais. We were told that a swash plate had been long overdue to be replaced on Darryl’s huey. If this breaks in flight a pilot will lose control of the aircraft. Not true according to Trevor Abrahams.

TREVOR ABRAHAMS: In terms of the swash plate, we are informed that the particular hour limitations on that swash plate was permissible and that wasn’t exceeding its time.

The ex-employee claims to have been at a meeting on the 24th of June 2015, with 2 CAA inspectors in Nelspruit. One of the things revealed to them was that kishugu had been buying components such as ball bearing and hydraulic hoses for their aircrafts from local manufacturers. If true, this would be illegal.

TREVOR ABRAHAMS: There is absolutely no evidence of those bearing being placed on aircraft.

JOHN: So what would they be bought for do you think?

TREVOR ABRAHAMS: Well the general bearings in terms of a whole lot of mechanical apparatus that we use, that’s where they can be applied.

But in Darryl Rea's notebook which was recently discovered by his wife Angela, there is an entry about this under a heading of maintenance problems:

We quote: "…… getting parts from local engineering shops – becoming commonplace now and accepted – illegal repairs using non aviation certified parts.

Two months after the alleged meeting between the ca and the ex employee, the CAA temporarily grounded the WOF fleet for their failure to comply with legislative requirements. NOW there is still no CAA report on Richard ashenbornes accident and Darryl Rea's accident report has still not been published but Bees Marais' has been, and its not very flattering.

LINK: In November 2015 the Civil Aviation Authority released a report into the Bees Marais accident in which damning findings were made around maintenance but just a few months later Trevor Abrahams authored a report of his own in which he rejected those findings and called on the minister of transport to review the investigation.

The CAA report found that the accident was likely caused when the control cable snapped, resulting in the failure of the tail rotor drive shaft. It's believed the cable was already fraying prior to the accident and should have been picked up by maintenance staff during regulated inspections.

TREVOR ABRAHAMS: We emphatically rejected that because they did not even interview the engineer which maintained that plane the day before the accident with the pilots present, including the deceased pilot.
JOHN: How do you know that?
TREVOR ABRAHAMS: We have an affidavit to that effect.


We asked Abrahams if we could speak to one of those pilots. He denied our request as he he did not want to interfere with judicial proceedings. An inquest into Bees’s death still has still not been conducted.

Abrahams and his team consulted with overseas experts for their own investigation and concluded that the cable was severed by a rotor blade during the crash. They said the CAA report was fundamentally flawed because certain evidence was ignored and some witnesses were not interviewed.

But late last year transport minister Dipuo Peters wrote back to Trevor Abrahams denying his request for a reopening of the investigation. She said, and we quote - there is no indication from your submission that the existence of these witnesses was bought to the attention of the investigator in charge.

Now, Abrahams is taking the minister’s decision on judicial review.

Working on fire provides an invaluable service and their pilots remain heroes but Jannie Smith strikes a cautionary note.

JANNIE: One must remember, these crashes that there were with Hueys in the firefighting, these will not be the last crashes. There'll be more incidence because of the danger and the nature of what they're doing

Pilots and their families understand the hazards of the jobs but are reliant on an entire team to give them the best chance of flying safely. Angela, she still has many unanswered question.

ANGELA: Because I lost my husband. You know he is the man, the love of my life, my little babies father and its just so unnecessary.

Working on fire is currently outsourcing their helicopters to four additional aircraft maintenance organisations as the need arises. In an email to us, Trevor Abrahams said that “we are resolute in our determination to uncover any systemic, maintenance, personnel or organizational issues, which may have contributed to these tragic events. The process is ongoing as it is in all the aviation industry.

TREVOR ABRAHAMS: Well the general bearings in terms of a whole lot of mechanical apparatus that we use, that’s where they can be applied. But in Darryl Rea's notebook which was recently discovered by his wife Angela, there is an entry about this under a heading of maintenance problems: We quote: "…… getting parts from local engineering shops – becoming commonplace now and accepted – illegal repairs using non aviation certified parts. Two months after the alleged meeting between the ca and the ex employee, the CAA temporarily grounded the WOF fleet for their failure to comply with legislative requirements. NOW there is still no CAA report on Richard ashenbornes accident and Darryl Rea's accident report has still not been published but Bees Marais' has been, and its not very flattering. LINK: In November 2015 the Civil Aviation Authority released a report into the Bees Marais accident in which damning findings were made around maintenance but just a few months later Trevor Abrahams authored a report of his own in which he rejected those findings and called on the minister of transport to review the investigation. The CAA report found that the accident was likely caused when the control cable snapped, resulting in the failure of the tail rotor drive shaft. It's believed the cable was already fraying prior to the accident and should have been picked up by maintenance staff during regulated inspections. TREVOR ABRAHAMS: We emphatically rejected that because they did not even interview the engineer which maintained that plane the day before the accident with the pilots present, including the deceased pilot. JOHN: How do you know that? TREVOR ABRAHAMS: We have an affidavit to that effect. We asked Abrahams if we could speak to one of those pilots. He denied our request as he he did not want to interfere with judicial proceedings. An inquest into Bees’s death still has still not been conducted. Abrahams and his team consulted with overseas experts for their own investigation and concluded that the cable was severed by a rotor blade during the crash. They said the CAA report was fundamentally flawed because certain evidence was ignored and some witnesses were not interviewed. But late last year transport minister Dipuo Peters wrote back to Trevor Abrahams denying his request for a reopening of the investigation. She said, and we quote - there is no indication from your submission that the existence of these witnesses was bought to the attention of the investigator in charge. Now, Abrahams is taking the minister’s decision on judicial review. Working on fire provides an invaluable service and their pilots remain heroes but Jannie Smith strikes a cautionary note. JANNIE: One must remember, these crashes that there were with Hueys in the firefighting, these will not be the last crashes. There'll be more incidence because of the danger and the nature of what they're doing Pilots and their families understand the hazards of the jobs but are reliant on an entire team to give them the best chance of flying safely. Angela, she still has many unanswered question. ANGELA: Because I lost my husband. You know he is the man, the love of my life, my little babies father and its just so unnecessary. Working on fire is currently outsourcing their helicopters to four additional aircraft maintenance organisations as the need arises. metadata.Summary: Last year a Working on Fire huey helicopter crashed whilst fighting fires. A week later, another one went down, also killing the pilot. Recently the CA released their findings on the cause for the first accident which is resulting in the deceased pilot's wife contemplating legal action. It found that working on fire maintenance was not up to scratch and that the pilot erred in not doing preflight checks and acting quickly when a light came on in the cockpit warning of gearbox failure. The CA report is being challenged by Working on Fire. We unpack the report using other experts such as a veteran helicopter pilot who has fought fires often himself. He will use his own huey helicopter as an example when chatting about the accidents and the report. For example the report says that the pilot should have noticed frayed cables but these are actually hidden underneath panels. Our case study Mr Jannie Smit will demonstrate this. He will also take us for a spin in his huey helicopter where some of the interviews will be done. This investigation will be set within a narrative about the huey helicopter and why they are so popular in South Africa. But they are controversial which we will touch upon. Our pilot will tell us that there is little doubt that in massive fires like the Cape has witnessed, it is little wonder that these huey helicopters experience extreme stress and that maintenance has to be a priority. The pilot continues to say that more fire fighting helicopter pilots will die because a lot of them lack the experience in firefighting. Right after the accident, the working on fire huey helicopters were grounded and all had to be checked, now maintenance is spread over several other companies, but the question remains: Working on Fire has massive contracts from thr govt. How is it possible that they only had 2 registered engineers whose job was to cover and inspect all 20 huey Helicopters? Was this cost saving?
